section.title: God the Righteous Judge
section.sectionRationale: A psalm of Asaph cast as a covenant lawsuit: God the Judge summons heaven and earth as witnesses, then addresses first His covenant people about the true nature of worship, and then the wicked about their empty profession. It teaches that God needs nothing from His people's sacrifices; He desires a thankful, obedient heart.
section.thesis: God, the divine Judge, does not need Israel's sacrifices for His own sustenance; He desires a thankful and obedient heart, and He will one day judge both covenant people and the wicked according to truth.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the theophany where God summons all the earth to judgment; His word to the covenant people about true worship; His rebuke of the wicked's hypocrisy; and a closing call to consider this, or be torn apart, paired with the promise of salvation to the one who walks rightly.

units.label: The Mighty One, God the LORD, speaks
units.note: the theophany that summons the earth

verses.text:
The Mighty One, {{elohim|God}} the LORD, speaks and summons the earth 
from where the sun rises to where it sets.
From Zion, perfect in beauty, God shines forth.

Our God approaches and will not be silent! Consuming fire precedes Him, 
and a tempest rages around Him.
He summons the heavens above, and the earth, that He may judge His people:
“Gather to Me My saints, who made a {{berith|covenant}} with Me by sacrifice.”
And the heavens proclaim His righteousness, for God Himself is Judge. Selah

units.label: I do not rebuke you for your sacrifices
units.note: the word to the covenant people about true worship

verses.text:
“Hear, O My people, and I will speak, O Israel, and I will testify against you: 
I am God, your God.
I do not rebuke you for your sacrifices, and your burnt offerings are ever before Me.
I have no need for a bull from your stall or goats from your pens,
for every beast of the forest is Mine, the cattle on a thousand hills.
I know every bird in the mountains, and the creatures of the field are Mine.
If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is Mine, and the fullness thereof.
Do I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?
Sacrifice a {{todah|thank offering}} to God, and fulfill your vows to the Most High.
Call upon Me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you will honor Me.”

units.label: What right have you to recite My statutes
units.note: the rebuke of the wicked's hypocrisy

verses.text:
To the wicked, however, God says, “What right have you to recite My statutes 
and to bear My covenant on your lips?
For you hate My instruction and cast My words behind you.
When you see a thief, you befriend him, and throw in your lot with adulterers.
You unleash your mouth for evil and unharness your tongue for deceit.
You sit and malign your brother; you slander your own mother’s son.
You have done these things, and I kept silent; you thought I was just like you. But now I rebuke you and accuse you to your face.

units.label: He who sacrifices a thank offering honors Me

verses.text:
Now consider this, you who forget God, lest I tear you to pieces, 
with no one to rescue you:

He who sacrifices a thank offering honors Me, and to him who rights his way, 
I will show the salvation of God.”

elohim.gloss: Verse 1 stacks three names for God together, the Mighty One, God, the LORD, an emphatic opening that leaves no doubt this is the sovereign covenant God Himself who comes to judge, not a lesser power.

berith.gloss: Covenant, a binding relationship sealed by sacrifice. God gathers His saints as those bound to Him by covenant, the same word used of His covenants with Abraham, Israel at Sinai, and finally the new covenant sealed in Christ's blood.

todah.gloss: Thank offering, an offering of gratitude rather than mere obligation. God repeats this word at the psalm's center and its close, verses 14 and 23, insisting that a thankful heart, not the sacrifice's material value, is what truly honors Him.

basic.context: Asaph pictures God arriving as Judge in a blazing theophany, summoning heaven and earth as witnesses against His own covenant people. God is not angry that Israel offers sacrifices; He is angry that they think He needs them, as though He were hungry and dependent on their rituals. What He wants is a thankful heart and a life that calls on Him honestly in trouble. Then He turns to the wicked, who recite His statutes with their lips while living in complicity with thieves and adulterers, and warns them plainly.
basic.hermeneutics: This is covenant lawsuit language, common in the prophets, where God brings a legal case against His own people for hollow religion. It should not be read as rejecting sacrifice itself, God ordained the sacrificial system, but as correcting the notion that ritual alone, without a grateful and obedient heart, can satisfy Him.
basic.originalLanguages: The opening verse stacks three names for God, El, Elohim, YHWH, an unmistakable declaration that the sovereign covenant Lord Himself is speaking. He calls His people to Him by berith, covenant, and twice insists that a todah, a thank offering from a grateful heart, is what truly honors Him, not the material sacrifice by itself.
basic.typology: God's insistence that He needs nothing from animal sacrifice, only a thankful and obedient heart, anticipates the once for all sacrifice of Christ, after which the only offering left for His people to bring is the sacrifice of praise and a life rightly lived.
basic.christ: Jesus is the true and final Judge this psalm anticipates, before whom all peoples will one day stand, John 5:22, Matthew 25:31-32. He also fulfills what this psalm demands beyond ritual: a life and death that is itself the perfect thank offering, so that His people now offer, through Him, a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name, Hebrews 13:15.
basic.god: God is shown as utterly self-sufficient, needing nothing from His creatures, yet still desiring relationship with them, calling for gratitude and honesty in trouble rather than empty religious performance. He is also the impartial Judge who holds His own covenant people to a higher account than anyone else.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Samuel 15:22 says to obey is better than sacrifice. Hosea 6:6 declares God desires mercy, not sacrifice. Hebrews 13:15 calls believers to offer a continual sacrifice of praise through Jesus. John 5:22 shows the Father has given all judgment to the Son.
basic.oneStory: God, the righteous Judge, needs nothing His people can offer Him; He desires a thankful, honest heart. That desire finds its answer once for all in Christ, the perfect thank offering, through whom His people now offer the sacrifice of praise while they wait for Him to come again as Judge of all the earth.

context.literary:
The psalm is a courtroom drama in three movements, and each movement changes the person addressed. Verses 1 to 6 are told in the third person, a herald's report of a summons that sweeps from sunrise to sunset. Verses 7 to 15 turn to the second person and speak to 'My people'. Verses 16 to 21 turn again, to a single class called 'the wicked'. Verses 22 and 23 close with a two sided appeal, a threat for those who forget God and a promise for the one who honors Him. The voice changes with the audience. The psalmist introduces the Judge, and from verse 7 to the end the Judge Himself speaks, which is a long stretch of direct divine speech for a psalm.

The stage is arranged with care. God speaks to the whole earth, verse 1, yet He shines from Zion, verse 2, and the case concerns His own covenant partners, verse 4. The witnesses are heaven and earth, verses 4 and 6, the same jurors Moses summoned in Deuteronomy 32:1 and Deuteronomy 4:26, and which Isaiah calls again in Isaiah 1:2. Micah 6:1-2 uses the same courtroom with mountains and hills as the jury. The prophets use the same form, but here it appears in a song sung in worship.

Two threads tie the halves together. The first is the verb honor. Deliverance in the day of trouble ends with 'you will honor Me', verse 15, and the last verse begins 'He who sacrifices a thank offering honors Me'. The lawsuit opens and closes its practical teaching on that one note. The second thread is the mouth. The worshippers are told to call on God, verse 15. The wicked have 'My covenant on your lips', verse 16, and the same mouth is then loosed for evil and deceit, verse 19. Verse 13 is a pair of blunt questions, and the irony is deliberate: the people who thought they were feeding God are asked whether He eats meat.

The psalm also sharpens as it goes. The first accusation is gentle, since God says He does not rebuke them for sacrifices. The second is severe, and it ends with the threat of being torn to pieces and the words 'with no one to rescue', verse 22.
context.historical:
Asaph appears in Chronicles as the Levite David set over the musicians ministering before the ark, sounding the cymbals, 1 Chronicles 16:4-7. He is also called a seer, and Hezekiah's Levites later sang his words alongside David's, 2 Chronicles 29:30. His descendants formed a guild of singers who 'prophesied' with harps and cymbals, 1 Chronicles 25:1. Psalm 50 is the only Asaph psalm in the second book of the Psalter; the others gather in Psalms 73 to 83. It matters that the rebuke comes from a member of the worship staff. The warning against hollow ritual comes from the inside of the sanctuary and not from a critic outside it.

The scene recalls the founding of the covenant. Verse 5 speaks of those who 'made a covenant with Me by sacrifice', and that is exactly what Moses did at Sinai, when young men offered burnt offerings and peace offerings and Moses sprinkled blood on the people, Exodus 24:5-8. The fire and storm of verse 3 belong to Sinai too, Deuteronomy 4:24 and Deuteronomy 33:2. What has changed is the mountain. The God who once shone forth from Sinai and Paran now shines from Zion, and Lamentations 2:15 remembers Jerusalem as 'the perfection of beauty', the same idea as 'perfect in beauty' in verse 2. Many scholars think a festival of covenant renewal, where the terms were rehearsed and the people warned, is the natural home for a psalm like this, though the text does not name the occasion.

The temple cult also had to be distinguished from the religion next door. In the surrounding nations, temple service was commonly understood as caring for the gods, with daily meals set before their images. Verse 12, 'If I were hungry, I would not tell you', is a direct denial of that picture. Israel's own offerings were never meant to feed God. In the thank offering the worshipper and family ate the meat themselves on the day it was offered, Leviticus 7:15, and God received the praise.

The accusations of verses 18 to 20 run through the second table of the law: theft, adultery, and a tongue used for deceit and for slandering one's own kin. The people addressed are covenant members who had memorised the terms and broke them, which is why Paul could later use the same charges against a religious person in Romans 2:21-24.
context.canonical:
Psalm 50 belongs to a chain of texts that hold sacrifice and obedience together without letting either swallow the other. Samuel told Saul that obedience is better than sacrifice, 1 Samuel 15:22. Hosea heard God say 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings', Hosea 6:6. Isaiah 1:11-17 has God tired of a multitude of offerings while the worshippers' hands are full of blood, and Micah 6:6-8 answers the question 'with what shall I come' with justice, mercy and humility. Among the psalms, Psalm 40:6-8, Psalm 51:16-17 and Psalm 69:30-31 all say that praise and a broken heart please God more than an ox or a bull. Psalm 50 is the fullest statement of the set, because it adds God's ownership of every animal and puts the rebuke in His own mouth.

The New Testament takes up the pattern at once. Jesus quotes Hosea twice in answer to those who valued ritual correctness above people, Matthew 9:13 and Matthew 12:7. He quotes Isaiah's charge of lips near and hearts far, Matthew 15:8-9, which is exactly the situation of verse 16. The letter to the Hebrews reads Psalm 40 as the words of Christ and concludes that God's will was done in the offering of a body, Hebrews 10:5-10, and then turns to the believer's part: 'Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name', Hebrews 13:15, together with doing good and sharing, Hebrews 13:16. Paul's call to present the body as a living sacrifice, Romans 12:1, and his preaching at Athens that God 'is not served by human hands, as if He needed anything', Acts 17:24-25, both stand on verses 9 to 12 of this psalm. Paul's line 'the earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof', 1 Corinthians 10:26, quotes Psalm 24:1, and Psalm 50:12 uses the same phrase in the mouth of God.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Asaph wrote to people who were doing everything the liturgy asked and still had a problem. The psalm was meant to be heard in the temple courts, with sacrifices at hand, and to make the worshippers ask what they thought they were doing. The first hearers were to take away a correction of their picture of God. He is the owner of every animal on a thousand hills, so no offering could ever supply something He lacked, verses 10 to 12. What He seeks is a relationship in which His people cry to Him in trouble, receive rescue, and give back thanks that is spoken and paid, verses 14 and 15. Sacrifice has meaning as an act of that relationship and none apart from it.

The second half was meant to unsettle the comfortable. To recite the statutes while quietly joining thieves and slanderers is a form of taking the covenant name lightly. The psalm states its cause: God's patience had been read as approval, verse 21, and the hearers were meant to see that silence is not consent. The psalm ends on both a warning and an open door, so that even the hypocrite is invited to become the person who 'honors Me'.

Asaph also gives a picture of what right worship looks like. It is thankful, it is honest in distress, and it is joined to a life that agrees with the words.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm reports a speech of God and records the charges He brings. It does not command a change in the cult on its own authority, and it does not tell anyone to stop offering sacrifices; the offerings of verse 8 are acknowledged as continual and are not condemned. What it prescribes is a right understanding of them and a matching life. The details of the accusation, the thief, the adulterer, the slanderer, are described as the conduct God knows about and not offered as a complete list of sins.

For Christians the sacrificial system is fulfilled, so the application is carried across rather than copied. The thank offering becomes the 'sacrifice of praise' of Hebrews 13:15. The trouble is real, and the invitation to 'call upon Me in the day of trouble' is a promise to be prayed, not a bargain to be worked. The warning to the wicked applies to anyone who carries the Bible and the name of Christ while keeping company with what the Bible condemns, and Jesus' teaching that gifts wait until a brother is reconciled, Matthew 5:23-24, shows how seriously He took it.

debates.question: Does the psalm reject the sacrificial system, or only its abuse?

views.label: It corrects a misuse and keeps the institution
views.case: God Himself gave the offerings, and verse 8 says He does not rebuke Israel for them, adding that the burnt offerings are 'ever before Me'. The complaint is aimed at the idea that sacrifice supplies God's needs or puts Him in the worshipper's debt, verses 9 to 13. On this reading the thank offering and the vow, verse 14, are commanded worship inside the same system.

views.label: It shows the system was always a shadow
views.case: If God needs no bull or goat, then the blood of animals was never the real payment. Hebrews draws that conclusion from Psalm 40, saying it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins, Hebrews 10:4, and that the first offering is removed to establish the second, Hebrews 10:9. Psalm 50 is read as one of the places where the Old Testament itself points beyond its own rituals.

debates.bearing: The two views are not rivals. Israel was to offer what God commanded, and it was to know that the offering was pointing beyond itself, to a thankful heart and finally to the perfect sacrifice of Christ. What neither view allows is ritual for its own sake.

debates.question: Who are the two groups in verses 7 to 21?

views.label: Two kinds of people
views.case: Verses 7 to 15 are for the faithful who bring sacrifices but have a wrong idea of them, and verses 16 to 21 are for the openly lawless who still use religious words. The change of address in verse 16, 'To the wicked, however', supports a real turn in audience.

views.label: One community seen from two sides
views.case: The same covenant people can be corrected for their attitude to the altar and exposed for their conduct beyond it. The wicked of verse 16 are not outsiders, since they bear the covenant on their lips, and the fault in both cases is worship divided from obedience. Some add that recitation of the statutes fits teachers and leaders in particular.

debates.bearing: Either way the hearer is not allowed to sit as a spectator. Each person is placed in the dock. A covenant member can be right in form and wrong in the heart, and a person can know the words of the law and keep company with those who break them.

debates.question: How can the psalm promise 'the salvation of God' to the one who 'rights his way'?

views.label: Salvation is earned by a changed life
views.case: Taken alone, verse 23 seems to make a righteous way the condition for God's salvation, and some readers have treated it as a plain principle of reward for conduct.

views.label: The changed life is the fruit of grace already given
views.case: The order of verses 14 and 15 shows that God delivers first and the worshipper responds with honor. The people are already addressed as those in covenant with Him, verse 5. Paul reads the whole Old Testament that way, insisting that the righteous live by faith, Romans 1:17, and that the one who calls on the Lord will be saved, Romans 10:13.

debates.bearing: The psalm does not offer a way to buy rescue. It shows what rescued people look like: they give thanks aloud, keep their promises, and their lives fit their words.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 8 has a small word with a large meaning. God says the burnt offerings are 'ever before Me', and the Hebrew word underneath is tamid, 'continually', the word used for the daily burnt offering that was to be made morning and evening for all generations, Exodus 29:38-42. God is not scorning the daily service. He is acknowledging it, and it is precisely His acceptance of the routine that makes the rebuke fall on the attitude and not on the act.

The thank offering of verses 14 and 23 comes from the family of the peace offerings. Leviticus 7:11-15 sets out the law of the peace offering, and its thanksgiving form was eaten by the worshipper on the day it was made. The verb for fulfilling vows in verse 14 is shallem, 'to pay, to make whole', from the same root as shelamim, the peace offerings. So the picture is a shared meal in which the giver pays what was promised, and God is host and not diner.

The promise of verse 15 has a close parallel in Psalm 91:15: 'I will deliver him and honor him.' In both places the pair is deliver and honor, and here the honor comes back to God from the people. The same verb for honor closes the psalm in verse 23, which is how the psalm frames itself.

In verse 16 the wicked 'recite' the statutes. The verb is the one used in Psalm 9:1, 'I will recount all Your wonders', and it means to tell out and count over. The wicked speak of the law the way a worshipper speaks of the wonders of God, and then 'bear' the covenant on their lips. The verb for bear is the one behind 'take the name of the LORD your God in vain' in Exodus 20:7, which suggests that carrying the covenant on an unfaithful mouth is a way of misusing the name.

In verse 17 they 'cast My words behind you', the same picture as Israel flinging the law 'behind their backs' in Nehemiah 9:26. In verse 18 the last line says the sinner's lot is with adulterers. The word for lot is the word for a person's portion, and the psalmists say of God 'The LORD is my chosen portion', Psalm 16:5. The covenant people were meant to have God for their portion, and these have taken the company of the lawless instead.

Verse 21 ends with the case being laid out before their eyes. The BSB footnote says the Hebrew is literally 'I set it in order before your eyes'. The verb is the one used for arranging wood and offering pieces in order on the altar, Leviticus 1:7-8, and for preparing a legal case, Job 13:18. The priest's care in laying out the sacrifice becomes God's care in laying out the evidence. The footnote to the same verse also records the reading 'you thought the I AM was like you', which some take as an echo of the name given at the bush, and which fits the charge that they made God in their own image.

typology.type: The thank offering as a shared meal, verses 14 and 23, Leviticus 7:11-15
typology.fulfillment: In the thank offering the worshipper ate before God, and God asked for the praise. That pattern reaches its climax at the table of Jesus, who 'gave thanks' before breaking the bread, Luke 22:19, and whose people are those who share in 'a participation in the blood of Christ', 1 Corinthians 10:16-18. Paul sets the Lord's Supper beside Israel's sacrificial meals for that reason. The type falls short because animals could only picture communion with God, while Christ's own body and blood make the fellowship real and permanent.

typology.type: The covenant made 'by sacrifice', verse 5, Exodus 24:5-8
typology.fulfillment: At Sinai Moses sprinkled the people with blood and said, 'This is the blood of the covenant'. Jesus takes those very words at the Last Supper, 'This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins', Matthew 26:28, and Hebrews 9:18-20 reads Sinai as the pattern for the new covenant. The escalation is from a covenant that promised obedience, and needed blood to hold it, to one that gives the forgiveness and the changed heart that obedience requires. The old covenant blood could not remove sin, Hebrews 10:4.

typology.type: Zion as the place where God shines forth, verse 2
typology.fulfillment: Sinai was the mountain of fire that the people were afraid to touch, and Zion was where God had chosen to dwell with His people. Hebrews says the church has come to a better Mount Zion, 'the heavenly Jerusalem', to 'God the Judge of all' and to Jesus the mediator, Hebrews 12:22-24, and it adds that 'our God is a consuming fire', Hebrews 12:29, quoting the same fire of Psalm 50:3. The type is limited to a hill in Judah, and Zion in Christ is the assembly of those from every nation who are gathered to Him.

typology.type: The summoning of heaven and earth to witness the Judge, verses 1 to 6
typology.fulfillment: The scene of verses 4 to 6 finds its end in the Son. The Father 'has assigned all judgment to the Son', John 5:22, and God has set a day 'when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed', Acts 17:31, so that each believer must 'appear before the judgment seat of Christ', 2 Corinthians 5:10. The psalm gives the pattern of a righteous trial of God's own household, and the New Testament names the Judge. The pattern falls short in that the psalm does not say how the guilty can be pardoned, which Christ's death answers.

study.christ:
Psalm 50 does not mention a Messiah, so the way to Christ has to be traced by the texts that take up its themes. The most direct is Hebrews 10:5-10. There Christ speaks the words of Psalm 40:6-8, 'Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but a body You prepared for Me', and the writer concludes that by God's will 'we have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all'. Psalm 50 says the same thing from the other side. God has no need of bulls and goats, so the sacrifice He accepts must come from somewhere else, and Hebrews says it came from the Son who came to do His will.

The Judge of the opening verses is one whom the New Testament identifies. Jesus says the Father 'has assigned all judgment to the Son', John 5:22, and Acts 17:31 names 'the Man He has appointed'. The psalm's thunder and fire announce a coming of God to judge, and the New Testament says that coming has a human face. That is a warning and a comfort. It is a warning because the audience of Psalm 50 is the covenant people and not pagans, and the same is true of the church, where, as Peter says, it is time for judgment to begin 'with the family of God', 1 Peter 4:17. It is a comfort because the One who will judge is the One who has already stood in the place of the guilty. Verse 22 speaks of being torn to pieces with 'no one to rescue', and the New Testament tells of a Judge who took that abandonment on Himself, crying out from the cross, Matthew 27:46, so that those who call on Him need never hear it, 2 Corinthians 5:21.

The thank offering finds a living form in Jesus. Luke tells of ten lepers cleansed, and of the one, a Samaritan, who came back 'praising God in a loud voice' and fell at Jesus' feet 'in thanksgiving to Him', Luke 17:15-16. Jesus asks where the other nine are. He receives the man's thanks as the offering God asks for in verse 14. At the Supper He 'gave thanks' over the bread, Luke 22:19, which is the source of the church's name for the meal, the Eucharist, meaning thanksgiving. Through Him, the believer's praise becomes 'a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name', Hebrews 13:15.

The psalm also sets a standard the covenant people did not keep and Christ did. The wicked recite the statutes and hate instruction. Jesus, in the words of Psalm 40:8, could say 'Your law is within my heart', and lived it. He is the one whose lips and life agree. A caution is in order: the psalm should not be read as though the bulls and goats were secret pictures of Christ in every detail. The links here rest on the psalm's own argument and on how Hebrews and the Gospels use it.
study.god:
The God of Psalm 50 owns everything and needs nothing. Every beast of the forest and the cattle on a thousand hills belong to Him, verse 10, and He knows every bird of the mountains, verse 11. This is the teaching that theology later called aseity, God's independence and self-sufficiency, and Paul gives it its plainest form at Athens: God 'is not served by human hands, as if He needed anything, because He Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else', Acts 17:25. The psalm makes the point in the most concrete way possible, by asking whether God eats bull's flesh.

Yet this self-sufficient God is not aloof. He calls the people 'My saints', verse 5, and 'My people', verse 7, and He asks to be called on, verse 15. The tension between His independence and His desire for relationship is resolved by the way the relationship runs. God is the giver, and worship is the answer. He does not need the gift, but He wants the thanks, and He wants it because it is true, since everything the people have was His to give. Ingratitude is not a small fault in this psalm. It is a form of the denial that He is who He says He is.

He is also a Judge in the fullest sense. Verse 6 says the heavens proclaim His righteousness 'for God Himself is Judge', and the BSB footnote gives the alternative 'He is a God of justice'. Fire goes before Him, verse 3, and the fire is the fire of a holy God who will not be reduced to a household deity. He is patient, verse 21 says, and He kept silent, yet verse 3 says 'Our God approaches and will not be silent'. The two verses do not contradict each other. Silence is the season of patience, and verse 3 is the end of it. Romans 2:4 says that God's kindness is meant to lead to repentance, and 2 Peter 3:9 says He is patient, not wanting anyone to perish. Ecclesiastes 8:11 shows the danger: when sentence is delayed, hearts become set on doing evil.

For worship the psalm asks three things of us. First, to see God as the giver and not as a recipient, so that we come with thanks and not with an attempt to earn credit. Second, to be truthful, since God can be trusted with our trouble and asks us to call on Him there. Third, to let our lips and our lives tell the same story. The God who rebukes hypocrisy is the same God who offers deliverance to those who call, and He says at the end that He will show 'the salvation of God' to the one who honors Him. Judgment and salvation are both real in Him, and neither cancels the other.

crossReferences.note: The covenant ceremony that verse 5 recalls. Burnt offerings and peace offerings were made, Moses read the Book of the Covenant, the people promised obedience, and the blood was sprinkled on them. The psalm addresses that same people generations later and asks whether the obedience they promised at the mountain is still in their lives.

Moses opens his song by calling on heaven and earth to listen, which makes them witnesses to the covenant. Psalm 50:4 and 6 summon the same witnesses. The parallel shows that this is a covenant lawsuit, and that the heavens and the earth have watched the whole history of Israel's response.

Micah asks with what he should come before the LORD, with year old calves or thousands of rams, and is told what is good: to act justly, love mercy and walk humbly with God. It carries the argument of verses 8 to 15 into the prophets, with the same courtroom setting opened in Micah 6:1-2.

God asks what good a multitude of sacrifices is to Him and tells the worshippers to wash, stop doing evil, and defend the fatherless and widow. The similarity to verses 16 to 21 is close, since both passages hold that sacrifice offered by hands that oppress is worthless.

The psalmist says that sacrifice and offering God did not desire, but that his ears were opened, and that he delights to do God's will. Psalm 50 states the negative side more sharply and Psalm 40 adds the positive, an obedient heart with the law within. Hebrews 10:5-10 reads it as Christ's own words.

David says that God takes no pleasure in burnt offerings, while a broken and contrite heart He will not despise. It is the same view of sacrifice as Psalm 50, put in the mouth of a guilty man and not of God the Judge, and it belongs to the same collection of lessons in true worship.

God promises to answer, be with the one in trouble, deliver him and honor him. Psalm 50:15 gives the same pattern of trouble, deliverance and honor, so the pair 'deliver' and 'honor' seems a standard way of describing the way of the Lord with His faithful.

The law of the peace offering and its thanksgiving form, with unleavened cakes and the rule that the meat be eaten the day it is offered. It shows that the thank offering of verses 14 and 23 was a meal the worshipper shared, and that it belonged to a festive fellowship and not to a transaction.

Paul tells the Athenians that God does not live in temples made by human hands and is not served by human hands as if He needed anything. It is the New Testament statement of Psalm 50:9 to 12, and shows how the early church carried the psalm's argument to a Gentile audience.

Jesus applies Isaiah's words about people who honor God with their lips while their hearts are far away. It matches the charge in verse 16 that the wicked carry the covenant on their lips, and shows Jesus reading the Old Testament as the fixed pattern of God's complaint against empty religion.

Paul asks the religious teacher whether he steals, commits adultery or robs temples while teaching others. The charges follow the pattern of verses 18 to 20, and Paul concludes that God's name is blasphemed because of them, which shows Psalm 50 still working as a warning in the age of the church.

When the sentence for a crime is not speedily carried out, hearts are set on doing evil. It explains the mechanism behind verse 21, where God's silence was read as approval, and shows why the coming of the Judge in verse 3 is both a threat and a mercy.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 50 begins where the Bible begins, with the God who owns the earth because He made it. 'Every beast of the forest is Mine' is Genesis 1 in the mouth of the Owner. It is also close to where the fall began, because Paul traces the human failure to a refusal of gratitude: 'although they knew God, they neither glorified Him as God nor gave thanks to Him', Romans 1:21. The psalm's hunger for a thank offering is not a small detail. It aims at the first disorder, a creature who takes God's gifts and forgets the Giver.

The middle of the story is the covenant. At Sinai a people was bound to God by blood, Exodus 24, and given the terms. The psalm stands in the long era between that promise and its fulfillment, when the people had the sacrifices and the law and still hearts unchanged. The prophets, Hosea, Isaiah and Micah, carry on the same lawsuit, and the exile is what the covenant curses look like in history. The psalm makes clear that the problem was never that God lacked enough sacrifices. The gift needed was a people who could truly give thanks and keep their word.

The psalm therefore leaves a question that only Christ answers. If God does not need bulls, and if the wicked cannot honor Him, who can offer the thanks and the obedience He seeks? The answer of Hebrews is the Son who came to do God's will, whose offering makes the people clean, Hebrews 10:10, and through whom they now offer a sacrifice of praise, Hebrews 13:15. The Judge of the psalm becomes the Savior, since the one appointed to judge, Acts 17:31, is the one who has borne the judgment.

The story ends in the presence of God. Revelation shows the great white throne, where the dead are judged according to what they have done, Revelation 20:11-12, and it also shows the multitude around the throne offering 'blessing and glory and wisdom and thanks and honor and power and strength', Revelation 7:12. The single word thanks belongs to the last chorus of creation. The thank offering of Psalm 50 has become the everlasting song of the redeemed, who honor Him in a world where no one needs to be warned to call on God, because He is present with them.

sermon.title: Call Upon Me in the Day of Trouble and I Will Deliver You
sermon.why: Piper works through Psalm 50's picture of God summoning heaven and earth as judge, and its call to true worship out of gratitude and honest dependence, showing the difference between empty ritual and a heart that truly calls on God in the day of trouble.

quiz.q: What kind of psalm is Psalm 50, in its overall shape?

options.text: A covenant lawsuit, with God as Judge summoning witnesses and addressing His people and the wicked in turn.
options.note: The theophany, summons of witnesses, and direct address to two groups match the classic covenant lawsuit pattern found also in the prophets.

options.text: A simple song of personal thanksgiving.
options.note: Thank offerings are discussed, but the psalm's overall shape is a legal summons and judgment scene, not a private thanksgiving song.

options.text: A love song for a royal wedding.
options.note: That describes Psalm 45, not Psalm 50.

options.text: A historical narrative retelling the exodus.
options.note: The exodus is not the subject here; the psalm is a courtroom-like scene set in the present, addressing worship and hypocrisy.

quiz.q: Why does God say He does not rebuke Israel for their sacrifices, yet still correct them (verses 8-13)?

options.text: Because they wrongly imagined God needed their offerings for sustenance, when the world and everything in it is already His.
options.note: Verses 9-13 make this explicit: God owns every animal and needs nothing from Israel's rituals.

options.text: Because their offerings were the wrong species of animal.
options.note: The text says nothing about incorrect species; the problem is the wrong view of why sacrifice is offered.

options.text: Because sacrifice itself had just been abolished.
options.note: The psalm does not abolish sacrifice; it corrects a wrong understanding of it.

options.text: Because they were not offering enough sacrifices.
options.note: Quantity is not the issue raised; the issue is the heart and understanding behind the sacrifice.

quiz.q: What does God specifically call for instead of, or alongside, ritual sacrifice (verses 14-15)?

options.text: A thank offering, fulfilled vows, and honestly calling upon God in the day of trouble.
options.note: Verses 14 and 15 state this directly as what truly honors God.

options.text: Total abandonment of the temple and priesthood.
options.note: The psalm does not call for this; it calls for a right heart within the existing covenant relationship.

options.text: Silence and the cessation of all prayer.
options.note: The opposite is true; God explicitly invites His people to call upon Him.

options.text: Larger and more costly sacrifices than before.
options.note: The emphasis is not on size or cost but on gratitude and honest dependence on God.

quiz.q: What specific hypocrisy does God rebuke in the wicked (verses 16-21)?

options.text: Reciting God's statutes and covenant with their lips while befriending thieves, adulterers, and slandering their own family.
options.note: Verses 16-20 list exactly this contradiction between profession and practice.

options.text: Refusing to attend temple worship at all.
options.note: The rebuke concerns those who do speak of God's covenant, but live in contradiction to it, not mere absence from worship.

options.text: Worshiping foreign gods openly.
options.note: The text does not describe idolatry here; it describes hypocritical profession alongside complicity with evil.

options.text: Giving too much money to the poor.
options.note: This is not mentioned; the rebuke concerns hypocrisy, not excessive generosity.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's demand for true worship find its fulfillment in Christ?

options.text: Christ offers the once for all sacrifice, after which His people offer God the sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name.
options.note: Hebrews 13:15 directly connects this pattern of praise-as-sacrifice to what Christ has accomplished.

options.text: Christ teaches that no sacrifice or offering of any kind is ever appropriate.
options.note: Scripture continues to call for offerings of praise and generosity even after Christ; the point is the heart behind them.

options.text: Christ replaces thankfulness with strict ritual obligation.
options.note: This reverses the psalm's and the New Testament's emphasis on grateful, willing worship over mere obligation.

options.text: Christ simply repeats the Old Testament sacrificial system without change.
options.note: Hebrews shows Christ's sacrifice as final and complete, not a mere repetition of the old pattern.

questions: God says He does not need Israel's sacrifices, because everything already belongs to Him. Where might you be treating your service to God as something He needs from you, rather than a grateful response to what He has already given?

God calls for a thank offering and honest calling upon Him in the day of trouble, rather than empty ritual. What would it look like this week to bring your real troubles honestly to God rather than performing religious routine?
The wicked in this psalm recite God's covenant with their lips while living in contradiction to it. Where is there a gap between what you profess about God and how you actually treat others?

God says He kept silent while the wicked sinned, and they mistakenly thought He was just like them. How does remembering that God's patience is not indifference change how you think about unaddressed sin in your own life?

The psalm closes with a promise, salvation shown to the one who rights his way. How does knowing Christ has already offered the perfect sacrifice change your motivation to live rightly, from fear to gratitude?

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew stacks three names for God together, El, Elohim, YHWH, an emphatic construction some versions render as 'The Mighty One, God, the LORD' to preserve the force of all three names appearing in sequence.
Made a covenant with Me by sacrifice recalls the sealing of the Sinai covenant in Exodus 24, where sacrifice ratified the relationship between God and His people.

Thank offering renders todah, a specific category of peace offering, Leviticus 7:12-15, offered in gratitude rather than for atonement, fitting the psalm's emphasis on a grateful rather than merely obligatory sacrifice.
